text: Could part of our vulnerability to joint disease be written into our evolutionary history? Researchers led by Kyoto University and the Weizmann Institute investigated DNA switches that regulate the human skeleton. They combined genome comparisons with experiments in cultured cells, then examined joint tissue. Their findings point to reduced activity in pathways involved in cartilage-maintaining molecules called glycosaminoglycans. These molecules help cartilage hold water and withstand pressure. The work offers a possible link between changes that shaped the human skeleton and its susceptibility to disease. But it does not identify a single cause of osteoarthritis, and it does not test a treatment. Human and ape cells were compared under experimental conditions; that is different from showing a benefit in patients. The value is a more detailed biological map that future research can investigate.
